title: GET vs POST
description: The complete comparison — data visibility, security, and when to use each method.
subject: html
html:
GET and POST are the two HTTP methods a form can use to submit its data — they solve genuinely different problems, and picking the wrong one is a real, common security and usability mistake.

Syntax

<form action="/search" method="get">
<form action="/login" method="post">

Basic Example

<!-- GET: data ends up in the URL -->
<form action="/search" method="get">
    <input type="search" name="q">
</form>
<!-- Submitting "python course" navigates to /search?q=python+course -->

<!-- POST: data is sent in the invisible request body -->
<form action="/login" method="post">
    <input type="password" name="password">
</form>
<!-- The password never appears in the URL at all -->

Browser output: both forms look identical on screen — the difference is entirely in how and where the data actually travels, invisible in the rendered page itself.

Full Comparison

GETPOST
Where data goesVisible in the URL as query parametersHidden in the request body
Bookmarkable / shareable?Yes — the full state is in the URLNo — the submitted data isn't part of the URL
Data size limitPractically limited by URL length (varies by browser, roughly 2000 characters is a safe rule of thumb)Effectively no practical limit for typical form data
Visible in browser history/server logs?Yes — a real privacy/security concernNo — meaningfully safer for sensitive data
Appropriate for...Search, filtering, anything safe to bookmark or repeatLogin, signup, payments, anything that changes data or is sensitive
File uploads?Not supportedSupported, with enctype="multipart/form-data"

The Security Reason This Really Matters

A GET request's data becomes part of the URL — meaning it's stored in browser history, can be logged by servers and proxies along the way, and can be accidentally shared just by copying the address bar's content. Never use GET for passwords, tokens, or any sensitive personal data.

Real-World Example

<!-- Correct: GET for a bookmarkable, shareable filter -->
<form action="/cources" method="get">
    <select name="category">
        <option value="ai">AI & Data Science</option>
    </select>
    <button type="submit">Filter</button>
</form>

<!-- Correct: POST for a sensitive, state-changing action -->
<form action="/change-password" method="post">
    <input type="password" name="new_password">
    <button type="submit">Update Password</button>
</form>

Two forms, two genuinely different, correct method choices — one benefits from being a shareable link, the other must never expose its data that way.

Common Mistakes

  • Using GET for a login form — the password would appear directly in the URL, browser history, and potentially server logs
  • Using POST for a simple search box, losing the ability for users to bookmark or share a specific search result URL

Best Practices

  • Use GET for safe, repeatable, shareable actions — search, filters, browsing
  • Use POST for anything sensitive, or anything that creates, updates, or deletes data

Accessibility Considerations

No direct accessibility impact — this is purely a data-transmission and security concern.

SEO Considerations

Search engines can crawl and index GET-based URLs (like filtered category pages) since the full state lives in the URL — a genuine advantage for filter/search pages that should be discoverable and indexable.

Browser & Modern HTML Notes

Both methods are core, foundational HTTP concepts, not HTML-specific — <form method="get/post"> is simply HTML's way of triggering the corresponding HTTP request type.

Mini Practice

  1. Decide GET or POST for: a course search box, a contact form, and a "delete my account" button.
  2. Explain, in your own words, why GET should never be used for a password field.

Module 7 Practice Lab

Quick Practice

Build a labeled login form: email input, password input (with correct autocomplete), and a submit button, using method="post".

Challenge

Take a signup form using only placeholders (no real labels) and no validation, and rewrite it with proper labels, required, pattern where relevant, and correct autocomplete values throughout.

Mini Project — Job Application Form

Build a complete job application form combining: a <fieldset>/<legend> for personal details (name, email, phone), a <fieldset> for a radio-button "preferred work mode" group, a <select> for "role applying for," a file input for resume upload (correct enctype), a <textarea> for a cover letter, a required "I agree to the Terms" checkbox, and a real <button type="submit"> — with every field properly labeled and validated.
